newsitem.title: UK: BOE seeks new chief economist to replace King.
newsitem.headline: BOE seeks new chief economist to replace King.

text.p: The Bank of England will soon be looking for a new chief economist to replace Mervyn King, and there are plenty of candidates for the influential position at the newly empowered central bank.

A Bank spokesman said on Thursday an appointment was not imminent as King would not vacate the post to become the central bank's second deputy governor in charge of monetary policy until later this year or early next.

"Mervyn King will carry on as chief economist until legislation creating the second deputy governor's position is passed, so a new chief economist will not be appointed in the near future," the spokesman said.
But he declined comment on speculation already circulating in London's financial district that an outsider would probably be sought for the post of chief economist.
The government said Dresdner Kleinwort Benson vice-chairman David Clementi would join the Bank on September 1 as deputy governor with responsibility for financial stability.
The chief economist wields considerable power at the Bank, with a vote at monetary policy committee meetings, and is widely considered to have the ear of the Governor on key interest rate decisions.

Overseeing the Bank's quarterly Inflation Report gives the chief economist a prominent platform to outline the Bank's thinking on economic developments. After the last report on May 13, sterling firmed sharply against the mark and dollar on King's comment that the Bank would have to seriously consider raising interest rates again.
"There is talk in the Bank that there is no credible candidate internally and it will have to go outside," said an economist with good contacts at the Bank.
"There is also a feeling that the chief economist should have a strong academic background, and not necessarily in monetary economics, so that means a wide field to choose from," he said.
A former Bank of England employee said an economist with a background in fiscal policy and microeconomics would be in with a good chance.
"Mervyn King was a fiscal policy expert and the Bank may want to carry on in that vein instead of choosing a monetary expert," said the former central bank employee.
King was a financial markets and tax specialist while professor of economics at the London School of Economics before joining the Bank in 1990.
Andrew Dilnott, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, and Charlie Bean, professor of economics at the London School of Economics, are both seen as possible contenders for King's post.
Bean is considered one of Britain's leading macro-economists, but his expertise in labour market and employment issues means he may be better suited to a position at the Treasury.
Bean's name has already been linked with Sir Alan Budd's job as chief economic adviser at the Treasury when Budd retires later this year.

He has also been linked with a position on the Council of Economic Advisers(CEA), the committee which will replace the largely-ignored "wise men" or panel of independent advisers to the Treasury set up by the last government.
News of appointments to the CEA is expected soon. -- London Newroom, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
